text.text: <atomic>One afternoon, Dave was playing lacrosse with his friend.</atomic>
<atomic>As he passed the ball, he wondered whether a ball's mass impacts how quickly it falls.</atomic>
<atomic>Since the force of gravity depends on an object's mass, Dave reasoned that a lacrosse ball would fall faster than a tennis ball, which has less mass.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this, Dave stood on a chair and dropped a lacrosse ball and tennis ball from the same height at the same time. His friend recorded the experiment on video. They repeated the procedure two more times.</atomic>
<atomic>They were surprised to see that each time, the lacrosse ball and tennis ball hit the ground at the same moment! Dave realized that his initial prediction was incorrect.</atomic>
<atomic>Instead, he hypothesized that all balls, regardless of their mass, fall at the same rate.</atomic>
<atomic>The next day, Dave shared his results with his physics class.</atomic>
<atomic>His teacher explained that all objects experience the same acceleration due to gravity, so they fall at the same rate when air resistance is negligible.</atomic>

imageLabel.text: a magnet attracting some paper clips

text.text: <atomic>During a lesson on magnets, Hannah's physics teacher explained that some materials are made up of microscopic areas called domains, which act like tiny magnets. If these domains align, the whole object is magnetized. If they point in random directions, their forces cancel out.</atomic>
<atomic>Hannah pondered whether temperature could affect a magnet's domains and overall strength.</atomic>
<atomic>Since heat increases particles' random movement, she reasoned that heating a magnet would randomize its domains and reduce its magnetism.</atomic>

<atomic>Hannah put a magnet in the freezer for 30 minutes. Then she held it above a pile of paper clips and counted the clips the magnet picked up. She then left the magnet at room temperature for 30 minutes and repeated these steps. Finally, she submerged the magnet in simmering water for 30 minutes and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>When she compared her results, Hannah found that the magnet picked up the fewest paper clips when hot and the most when cold.</atomic>
<atomic>She deduced that higher temperatures make magnets weaker.</atomic>

imageLabel.text: using a wrench to remove a bolt from a tire

text.text: <atomic>Maddie watched her sister change a tire. One bolt seemed stuck, so she took a hollow pipe and put it over the wrench's handle to make it longer.</atomic>
<atomic>Maddie wondered why this helped her sister remove the bolts.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the longer handle allows a person to use less force to turn the wrench.</atomic>

<atomic>To test her idea, Maddie and her sister drilled nine small bolts into a wooden board. Maddie then attached a spring scale to a normal wrench. As she pulled the spring scale at a right angle to turn the wrench, she measured the force it took to remove a bolt. She repeated this with two more bolts and averaged the three measurements. Then she put a short pipe over the handle and removed the next three bolts. Finally, she put a long pipe over the handle and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>When she compared the three averages, she found that the longest handle took the least force to remove the bolts, while the unmodified wrench took the most.</atomic>
<atomic>Maddie concluded that the longer a wrench's handle is, the less force it takes to turn it.</atomic>

imageLabel.text: a circuit containing a battery and a light bulb

text.text: <atomic>Noah just learned about Ohm's law in physics class. This law states that the current passing through a circuit is directly proportional to the voltage applied. He wondered what would happen if he connected the same light bulb to different batteries with different voltages.</atomic>
<atomic>Noah reasoned that increasing the voltage would increase the current in the circuit, so the light bulb would glow brighter.</atomic>

<atomic>Noah connected a small light bulb to a 3-volt battery using copper wires. The bulb lit up dimly. Then, he connected the same bulb to a 9-volt battery, and it shone much brighter. Lastly, Noah connected the bulb to a 12-volt battery. To his surprise, it flickered briefly and then stopped glowing.</atomic>
<atomic>Noah was confused, since the other circuits had behaved as predicted.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that there must be another factor to explain the bulb's behavior.</atomic>
<atomic>Noah told his physics teacher about his experiment, and she explained that light bulbs are designed for specific voltages. When that voltage is exceeded, the light bulb burns out.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Before practice, the members of the Oak Grove High School basketball team inflated the team's basketballs to a pressure of 8 pounds per square inch.</atomic>
<atomic>The team members wondered if the air pressure in the basketballs would affect bounciness.</atomic>
<atomic>They thought that if bounciness depended on air pressure, then basketballs inflated to a higher pressure would bounce higher.</atomic>
<atomic>The team members inflated ten basketballs to different pressures and dropped each ball three times from a ladder.</atomic>
<atomic>They measured how high the basketball bounced each time.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, they made a graph to see if the basketballs inflated to a higher pressure bounced higher.</atomic>
<atomic>From the graph, they concluded that the basketballs with a higher pressure were bouncier.</atomic>
<atomic>The team members shared their graph with other sports teams at their school.</atomic>
<atomic>The soccer team decided to test for the same pattern with soccer balls.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>In physics class, Miguel's teacher explained that suction cups stick because of air pressure—there is very little air between the suction cup and the surface it's pressed against, so the air around the suction cup pushes it against the surface.</atomic>
<atomic>Miguel pondered, then, how suction cups would perform in a vacuum.</atomic>
<atomic>If there were no air to push them against a surface, he supposed that suction cups would be ineffective.</atomic>

<atomic>Miguel got two large mason jars and six suction cups. After sticking three suction cups onto an inside wall of each jar, he laid both jars horizontally so that the suction cups were face down. He then used his parents' vacuum sealer to remove the air from one of the jars.</atomic>
<atomic>When he stood both jars up, he found that all the suction cups in the vacuum-sealed jar fell off immediately, while the others held!</atomic>
<atomic>He determined that suction cups cannot work in a vacuum.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One afternoon, Carmen was sliding a heavy book across her desk, and she noticed that it slid less easily across her desk mat than across the wooden desktop.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered how a surface's texture affects the way objects slide across it.</atomic>

<atomic>Carmen guessed that it would take less force to slide the book across her smooth tiled kitchen floor than to slide it across a rougher surface, like her desk mat or the living room carpet.</atomic>

<atomic>Carmen tied a spring scale to the book. She placed the book at the edge of her desk mat and pulled it using the spring scale, measuring the force it took to get the book to slide. She repeated this process twice. She then repeated the procedure on the tile floor and the carpet.</atomic>

<atomic>Finally, she calculated the average force needed to slide the book on each surface. She observed that it took the most force to slide it across carpet and the least force to slide it across tile.</atomic>
<atomic>Carmen concluded that the smoother the surface, the less force it takes to slide an object across it.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>In physics class, Polly learned that work is done when a force is applied over a distance.</atomic>
<atomic>Her teacher also mentioned that lifting a given mass a certain distance will always take the same amount of work. Polly wondered how work might relate to pulley systems.</atomic>
<atomic>If a pulley system reduces the force needed to lift an object, she reasoned, that force must be applied to a greater length of rope to do the same amount of work.</atomic>

<atomic>Polly set up a single pulley. She attached a spring scale to the end of the rope and marked where the rope connected to the pulley. She pulled the spring scale to lift a mass one meter off the ground and measured the force and the length of rope pulled through the pulley. She repeated the experiment with a two-pulley system and a three-pulley system.</atomic>
<atomic>She compared her measurements and found that each additional pulley reduced the force but increased the length of rope needed to lift the mass.</atomic>
<atomic>She determined that she was right—pulley systems that require less force require more rope.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Jane's dog, Ziggy, loved to play fetch.</atomic>
<atomic>When Jane threw balls for Ziggy, she noticed that different types of balls traveled different distances.</atomic>
<atomic>Jane wanted to know if the distance a ball traveled was related to its mass.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that lighter balls would travel farther.</atomic>
<atomic>So, Jane bought seven rubber balls that were the same size but had different masses.</atomic>
<atomic>She used a ball launcher to launch each ball three times, using the same force with all the balls, and then she examined her results.</atomic>
<atomic>She deduced that there was a relationship between ball mass and distance traveled: the lighter a ball was, the farther it traveled.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared a description of her tests and a graph of her results with her friends at the dog park.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mary recently heard about acupressure mats, which are covered in small plastic spikes. Mary was surprised to learn that people find these mats comfortable—and even therapeutic.</atomic>
<atomic>She guessed that spreading a person's weight over a large number of spikes would decrease the pressure exerted by each spike.</atomic>

<atomic>Mary collected three identical balloons, some nails, three wooden boards, and a textbook. She then hammered one nail through the first board, nine nails in a grid measuring three inches by three inches through the second, and 36 nails in a grid of the same size through the last. Mary held the first balloon on the single nail and placed the textbook on top. The balloon popped instantly, suggesting that the nail exerted a lot of pressure. She held the next balloon on the grid of nine nails and placed the textbook on top. This time, the balloon took a moment to pop. Finally, Mary repeated the procedure with the 36-nail grid, and the balloon did not pop at all!</atomic>
<atomic>Mary determined that when weight is distributed over many spikes—like on an acupressure mat—each spike exerts only a small amount of pressure.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>At the playground, Meg's younger brother asked her to get on the seesaw with him. She sat down, and his seat immediately rose into the air. Meg found that when she scooted toward the middle of the seesaw, it seemed to even things out so that her brother came back down.</atomic>
<atomic>She remembered from physics class that levers such as seesaws experience torque, or rotational force, around their point of rotation.</atomic>
<atomic>Meg pondered how an object's distance from the point of rotation on a seesaw affects the torque it exerts.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that moving an object closer to the point of rotation on a seesaw would reduce the torque it exerts.</atomic>

<atomic>Meg made a miniature seesaw by balancing a meter stick on a cylindrical block. She put a 100-gram mass at each end of the meter stick, and they balanced perfectly. When she moved one mass halfway to the middle, she found that it rose up in the air. She repeated the experiment with two 150-gram masses and again with two 200-gram masses. In each case, she observed the same result.</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that moving an object closer to the point of rotation on a seesaw decreases the torque it exerts.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Julia pushed Emily and Emily's little brother, Mateo, on swings.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia noticed that Mateo always swung back in less time than Emily.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia asked Emily if she thought the weight on a swing was related to the time it took to return.</atomic>
<atomic>To find out, Emily stood back four feet and released a swing three times, once with a light weight attached to it, once with a medium weight, and once with a heavy weight.</atomic>
<atomic>Julia measured how long it took the swing to go forward and back each time.</atomic>
<atomic>They repeated the tests on ten swings.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that weight on a swing wasn't related to swinging time, since for each swing the time was similar with all three weights.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, Julia noticed that swings with shorter chains always swung back sooner.</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that chain length would determine swinging time and that shortening a swing's chains would shorten the time it took to swing back.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One day, Wendy was using a slingshot to launch pebbles at a target in her backyard. Sometimes the pebble hit the target with a loud thud, but other times it barely made a sound.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered whether this had to do with how far she stretched the slingshot band.</atomic>

<atomic>Wendy thought that stretching the band must build up its potential energy, which would then get transferred to the pebble. She guessed that stretching the band farther would launch the pebble farther.</atomic>

<atomic>Wendy gathered nine pebbles of about the same size and mass. She launched three pebbles by stretching the slingshot band a little, three more by stretching it moderately, and the final three by stretching it as far as possible. She measured how far each pebble traveled and calculated each group's average.</atomic>
<atomic>As expected, the pebbles traveled the farthest when she stretched the band as far as possible; they traveled the least when she stretched it a little.</atomic>
<atomic>Wendy concluded that stretching the band farther launches a pebble farther.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>In physics class, Ashley learned that friction is created when one object slides against another.</atomic>
<atomic>The amount of friction depends on the amount of force holding the objects together and the texture of the objects' surfaces. She wondered why her teacher didn't mention surface area.</atomic>
<atomic>It seemed to her that objects should experience more friction if they had larger surfaces touching.</atomic>

<atomic>Ashley found a wooden board and laid it down on the side with the greatest area. She secured a spring scale to one end of the board. Then she dragged the board across the floor three times, using the spring scale to measure the force needed to move it. Then she stood the board on its thin edge and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>Finally, she calculated the average force for each orientation. She found that the averages were the same!</atomic>
<atomic>Ashley decided that her idea must have been wrong.</atomic>
<atomic>Instead, surface area must not affect friction.</atomic>
<atomic>She asked her teacher about her results, and he explained that increasing surface area reduces the pressure between the objects at every point, canceling out any effect.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>To introduce color theory, Gabe's science teacher gave each lab group three colored bulbs: one blue, one green, and one red. She instructed the groups to predict what colors the bulbs' lights would make when mixed.</atomic>

<atomic>Gabe's group reasoned that the colors should mix just like paint—red and green would make brown, blue and red would make purple, blue and green would make teal, and all three would make a dark brownish color.</atomic>
<atomic>To test their predictions, Gabe and his group shined their bulbs on the wall so that the colored light overlapped.</atomic>
<atomic>The resulting colors were not what the group had expected. Red and green made yellow, blue and green made cyan, blue and red made magenta, and all three made white!</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that they were wrong, and that colored bulbs must be different from paint.</atomic>
<atomic>All the groups shared their results, and their teacher explained that paint absorbs certain colors of light and reflects others, while bulbs produce certain colors of light.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Miles was helping his younger sister use a foam dart launcher that she received for her birthday.</atomic>
<atomic>They wondered what launch angle would cause the foam dart to travel the farthest horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They thought that launching with a higher angle to the ground would give the dart more time to travel before hitting the ground and would therefore allow the foam dart to travel farther.</atomic>

<atomic>Miles and his sister set up an experiment in their backyard. They used a protractor to adjust the launcher to five different angles: 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 75°. They launched three foam darts from each angle and used a measuring tape to determine how far each dart traveled horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They then calculated the average for each group and graphed the results. They found that the darts launched at 45° went the farthest, while those launched at 15° and 75° traveled the shortest distance.</atomic>
<atomic>Miles and his sister shared their results with the friend who had given his sister the launcher.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Kevin runs a catering business.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered where he should chill sodas for an event: in the fridge, a cooler filled with ice water, or a cooler filled with ice cubes.</atomic>

<atomic>He recalled that solids conduct heat better than liquids or gases, so he reasoned that the fridge should be the least effective, and the cooler with solid ice should be the most effective.</atomic>

<atomic>To test his idea, Kevin opened nine bottles of soda and measured their temperatures. He put three in the fridge, three in a cooler with ice water, and three in a cooler with ice cubes. He checked the sodas' temperatures every five minutes and compared them.</atomic>
<atomic>The sodas in the fridge cooled the slowest, as expected. But surprisingly, the sodas in the ice water cooled the fastest!</atomic>
<atomic>He realized that the solid ice did not touch the bottles' entire surface, while the ice water did.</atomic>
<atomic>Kevin revised his prediction: Encasing the sodas in a block of ice would cool them the most effectively, but it was more practical to use ice water.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his findings with his employees.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>During a lesson on magnets, Vicky's physics teacher explained that some materials are made up of microscopic areas called domains, which act like tiny magnets. If these domains align, the whole object is magnetized. If they point in random directions, their forces cancel out.</atomic>
<atomic>Vicky pondered whether temperature could affect a magnet's domains and overall strength.</atomic>
<atomic>Since heat increases particles' random movement, she reasoned that heating a magnet would randomize its domains and reduce its magnetism.</atomic>

<atomic>Vicky put a magnet in the freezer for 30 minutes. Then she held it above a pile of paper clips and counted the clips the magnet picked up. She then left the magnet at room temperature for 30 minutes and repeated these steps. Finally, she submerged the magnet in simmering water for 30 minutes and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>When she compared her results, Vicky found that the magnet picked up the fewest paper clips when hot and the most when cold.</atomic>
<atomic>She deduced that higher temperatures make magnets weaker.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Fred took his motorized toy boat to the park with his cousin.</atomic>
<atomic>The boat zipped across the pond, and Fred wondered if adding mass to the boat would affect its speed.</atomic>
<atomic>He didn't think so, since the motor should keep propelling it at the same rate.</atomic>

<atomic>Fred decided to time the boat as it traveled from one side of the pond to the other. He then taped a pebble to the boat and timed it again. Finally, he added a second pebble and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>Fred noticed that as he added mass, the trips took longer. The empty boat took the least time to cross the pond, and the boat with two pebbles took the longest.</atomic>
<atomic>Fred concluded that adding mass does slow down the boat.</atomic>
<atomic>He changed his prediction: The motor must provide a set amount of force, so it can't maintain the same speed as more mass is added.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results with his aunt and confirmed that the boat's motor exerts a consistent force, so increasing the boat's mass reduces its acceleration.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>David was building a solar-powered cart.</atomic>
<atomic>As he placed the solar panel on the top of the cart, he wondered how the angle of the solar panel would impact the voltage generated.</atomic>
<atomic>He recalled that he often saw rooftop solar panels set at an angle, and he reasoned that angling the solar panel 45° from the top of the cart would generate the greatest voltage.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this, he first laid the solar panel flat on the cart. He then turned on a ceiling light directly above the cart and used a voltmeter to measure the voltage generated. He repeated this with the solar panel angled at 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the solar panel generated the greatest voltage when it was flat against the cart.</atomic>
<atomic>David realized that the light source was directly above the solar panel, which is not always true for rooftop solar panels.</atomic>
<atomic>He now predicted that solar panels generate the greatest voltage when they are angled so that light hits the panel directly.</atomic>
<atomic>Later that week, David shared his findings with his engineering club at school.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Brenda was coaching tennis on a hot summer day. As she hit a ball that had been left on the court, she was surprised to find that it bounced more than the brand new ones she had just opened!</atomic>

<atomic>She thought that it must have something to do with the ball's temperature—the hot asphalt must have warmed it up and made it bouncier than the new ones that had been in an air-conditioned house.</atomic>

<atomic>To test the idea, Brenda and her friend gathered nine new tennis balls. They put three in the freezer, left three in the hot sun, and left the remaining three on the kitchen table at room temperature. Thirty minutes later, Brenda took all the balls and dropped each one from the top of a 10-foot ladder. Her friend measured how high each one bounced.</atomic>
<atomic>They found that the heated tennis balls bounced the highest, while the frozen ones bounced the lowest.</atomic>
<atomic>They concluded that tennis balls must become bouncier as their temperature rises.</atomic>
<atomic>The next day, Brenda shared what she learned with her fellow coaches.</atomic>

Then, she put the heavier set of wheels on the car and rolled down the hill three more times. Once again, she measured how long it took to reach the bottom of the hill each time. Finally, she calculated the average time for each set of wheels.

mainText.text: Bruce recently heard about acupressure mats, which are covered in small plastic spikes. Bruce was surprised to learn that people find these mats comfortable, even therapeutic. He guessed that distributing a person's weight over a large number of spikes would decrease the pressure exerted by each spike. To test this, Bruce collected three identical balloons, some nails, three wooden boards, and a stack of small books. He hammered nine nails in a grid measuring three inches by three inches through the first board, 16 nails in the same-sized grid through the second board, and 25 nails in the same-sized grid through the third board. Then, Bruce placed a balloon on each grid and laid a book on top of the balloon. He continued adding books until the balloon popped. The more books the balloon could support without popping, the less pressure exerted by each nail.
